title: Checking a found hammer, axe, maul or sledge
summary: A two-minute check before you swing a found hammer, axe, maul or sledge: a tight head, a sound handle and an undamaged face or edge. Heads fly off loose or cracked handles, and chipped or mushroomed faces throw steel.

steps.text: Put on safety glasses and gloves, and look the tool over in good light before you swing it at anything (CCOHS general, CCOHS hammers).
Scrape off dirt, pitch and loose rust with a scraper or a wire brush so cracks can show. Keep power tools away from an axe's cutting edge (Ax Manual ch13).
Hold the handle and try to twist and rock the head. Look for a gap round the handle at the eye and for the wedge in the top of the handle (CCOHS hammers, Ax Manual ch12).
steps.warn: Any movement means don't use it: a loose head can fly off and hit you or someone nearby (OSHA 3080, Council care).

steps.text: Run your eyes and hand along the handle: cracks, splits, splinters, crushed or rough wood, and grain that runs out the front or back. Look hardest just below the head, where handles break (CCOHS hammers, Ax Manual ch6, ch9).
On a steel- or fibreglass-handled hammer, look for dents, cracks and a loose grip; Estwing lists a dented handle as a reason to discard (Estwing safety).
Check a hammer, sledge or maul face: chips, cracks, dents, a mushroomed rim, and whether the bevel (chamfer) round the face is still there (CCOHS hammers, Estwing safety, Council care).
steps.warn: A chipped or mushroomed face can throw steel chips at the next blow. Don't grind, weld or reheat it (CCOHS hammers).

steps.text: On a claw hammer, check the claw and the eye for cracks (CCOHS hammers, Estwing safety).
On an axe or hatchet, check the edge for chips and a rounded toe, the poll for mushrooming, the eye for bulges, and the whole head for hairline cracks, especially round the eye (Ax Manual ch13).
Sight down the cutting edge of an axe to the knob at the end of the handle: they should line up (Ax Manual ch10).
Check any chisels, punches and wedges in the same box for mushroomed, chipped or cracked struck ends (CCOHS struck). See Striking hardened tools.
Sort each tool: use, repair (re-wedge or re-handle), or retire. Put retired heads away from the working tools so nobody grabs one in a hurry (CCOHS general, Council right tool).

notes:
## Why check
A found hammer, axe or sledge may have been stored wet, dry, hot or frozen, or misused. The hand-tool injuries OSHA lists are mostly about condition: a head that flies off a loose, splintered or cracked handle, and steel chips from a mushroomed head (OSHA 3080). CCOHS says to inspect every tool before use and repair or replace a faulty one (CCOHS general). Two minutes of looking saves an eye. Read [Striking hardened tools](#guides/safety_struck_tools) first; for axe sharpening and use see [Axe and hatchet care](#guides/skill_axe_care).

## The head on the handle
- **Tight.** The head must not move at all on the handle. Twist it and rock it; look for a gap round the handle at the eye. Replace a handle that is loose, cracked or splintered (CCOHS hammers, CCOHS general).
- **Wedge.** A wooden handle is held by a wedge driven into a slot (kerf) in its top. No wedge, a wedge that has backed out, or a split top means the head will work loose. Often only the wedge needs replacing (AATG hanging).
- **Shrunken handle.** Wooden handles shrink as they dry, more in hot, dry places (Ax Manual ch12). An axe kept beside a stove can come loose this way (Ax Manual ch12, Gränsfors care). Don't soak it in water to swell it: the swelling wood is crushed in the eye and the head ends up looser (Ax Manual ch12).
- **Pinned heads.** Some axes have a steel pin through the head and handle, low down in the eye, so a loose head can't fly off (Ax Manual ch10). A pin is a backstop, not a fix: a loose pinned head still needs re-wedging (Ax Manual ch12, CCOHS hammers).
- **Glued and epoxied heads** can come loose too: check them the same way (Gränsfors care).

## The handle itself
- Cracks, splits, splinters, crushed fibres and badly weathered or rough wood all mean a new handle (CCOHS hammers, Trail handles). Small surface checks from drying are normal on an old axe; watch whether they grow (Ax Manual ch12).
- The weak spot is just below the head, where the wood takes the shock of every blow and gets crushed and flexed (Ax Manual ch9).
- Grain should run the length of the handle, in line with the slot for the wedge. Grain that runs out on the front or back of the handle ("runout") is weak and likely to break (Ax Manual ch6, Trail handles).
- Paint or varnish can hide flaws; scrape a little off where you have doubts (Trail handles).
- Steel and fibreglass handles: Estwing tells you to discard a hammer whose handle is dented (Estwing safety). Fibreglass handles aren't made to be reshaped (Ax Manual ch6).

## Hammer, sledge and maul faces
| What you see | What to do | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Clean face, bevel (chamfer) intact | Use | CCOHS hammers |
| Sledge or maul face with only light wear | Council Tool: keep it up with a flat file, keeping the convex face and chamfer. Forest Service: grind lightly without overheating, because the temper is shallow. CCOHS: don't redress, grind, weld or re-heat-treat a hammer head. Don't file away a chip or a mushroomed rim: retire it | Council care, Trail tools, CCOHS hammers |
| Chips, cracks, dents, a mushroomed rim, heavy wear | Retire it as a striking tool | CCOHS hammers, Estwing safety, Council right tool |
| Crack in the claw or the eye | Retire it | CCOHS hammers, Estwing safety |

The bevel round the face is there for a reason: bevelled faces are less likely to chip or spall (CCOHS hammers). CCOHS says not to reshape, grind, weld or re-heat-treat a hammer head (CCOHS hammers); the Forest Service says to grind a sledge face only lightly, without overheating it, because the temper is shallow, and to have badly chipped or mushroomed faces reconditioned by a blacksmith (Trail tools); Council Tool says faces are best kept up with a flat file (Council care). Without a smith who can forge and re-harden it, a damaged face stays retired. Sledges are made in different tempers for different jobs and aren't interchangeable (Trail tools).

## Axe and hatchet heads
- **Edge.** Small chips file out if there is enough hardened steel left. A big chip, or a toe filed back until it is rounded, means re-profiling the whole edge, and filing too far back leaves the hardened zone for soft steel that won't hold an edge (Ax Manual ch8, ch13). The temper line, where you can see it, shows how much life is left (Ax Manual ch13).
- **Poll.** A rounded or mushroomed poll probably means someone drove steel wedges with it; the poll isn't hardened. Grind the mushroom back before use and then look for cracks; never strike with a poll that folds over, because its thin edges break off (Ax Manual ch13).
- **Eye.** A bulging or misshapen eye won't hold a handle properly and may keep changing shape and break (Ax Manual ch8, ch13).
- **Cracks.** Hairline cracks hide under dirt and rust, most often in the thin cheeks and at the points of the eye. Any crack in an axe head is dangerous. Welding a crack may not be worth the effort, and the Forest Service author says to discard a cracked head unless you have the skills to repair it safely (Ax Manual ch13).
- **Pitting.** Surface rust is fine; deep pitting at the edge leaves weak spots that chip or break (Ax Manual ch13).
- **Alignment.** Sight down the cutting edge: it should line up with the middle of the knob at the end of the handle (Ax Manual ch10).

## Retire or repair
| Finding | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Loose head, sound handle | Re-wedge ([re-handling](#guides/repair_tool_handle)) |
| Cracked, split or splintered handle | New handle ([re-handling](#guides/repair_tool_handle)) |
| Hammer or sledge face chipped, cracked, mushroomed | Retire (CCOHS hammers, Estwing safety) |
| Maul or splitting wedge with dents, cracks, chips, mushrooming or heavy wear | Council says discard (Council right tool) |
| Axe poll mushroomed, no cracks | Grind it back with care (it changes the balance), look again for cracks, then use (Ax Manual ch13) |
| Crack anywhere in a head | Retire (Ax Manual ch13, CCOHS hammers, CCOHS struck) |
